start.text:
The community midwife calls you urgently to the assessment room:

'Dr. — I need you now. I have Amara Okonkwo, 28 years old, G1P0, 34 weeks and 2 days. She walked in 20 minutes ago complaining of a headache for the past two days that paracetamol isn't touching. This morning she started seeing flashing lights and sparkles. Her face looks puffy. I'm really worried.'

You walk in. Amara is sitting upright on the examination bed, pressing her fingers to her temples. She is alert but clearly in pain. Her abdomen is gravid and appropriate for 34 weeks.

'I've had this headache since Tuesday,' she says quietly. 'And now my vision keeps going sparkly on the right side. I thought it was just tiredness.'

Midwife's initial observations: HR 86 | BP 162/108 | RR 16 | Temp 37.1°C | SpO₂ 99%

What is your first priority?

choices.text: Lay her on her left side and formally re-assess BP with correct technique — then take a targeted obstetric history

effects.reason: BP formally assessed with correct technique — essential first step in any pregnant patient presenting with headache and visual disturbances

choices.text: Reassure her — tension headaches and visual migraine are common in the third trimester and are usually benign

effects.reason: Reassuring a 34-week pregnant patient with headache, visual disturbances, and BP 162/108 without further assessment is dangerous. These are classical presenting features of preeclampsia with severe features.

choices.text: Give her stronger analgesics for the headache and ask the midwife to keep monitoring

effects.reason: NSAIDs are contraindicated after 20 weeks gestation. Treating the headache symptomatically without identifying the cause in a pregnant patient with BP 162/108 delays critical management and risks fetal harm.

choices.text: Order a urine dipstick immediately while the midwife takes a history — proteinuria is the critical diagnostic test

effects.reason: Urinalysis ordered immediately — excellent clinical instinct. Proteinuria combined with hypertension in pregnancy defines preeclampsia.

premature-dismissal.text:
You begin to reassure Amara or ask for analgesics.

The midwife steps closer and lowers her voice: 'I've been a community midwife for 14 years. I've seen preeclampsia twice before. I'm telling you — her BP was the same when I measured it 30 minutes ago, 158/106. Her feet are significantly swollen. And she has a headache that won't go with paracetamol, plus visual symptoms.

With respect, Doctor — I think you need to take her blood pressure properly yourself.'

She's right. You need to immediately reassess.

choices.text: The midwife is absolutely right — formally assess BP and take a proper obstetric history

effects.reason: BP formally assessed after appropriate clinical challenge

vitals-and-history.text:
Formal Assessment — Left lateral position, 5 minutes rest, validated digital sphygmomanometer:

BP measurement 1 (5 min): 162/108
BP measurement 2 (10 min): 164/106

Consistently elevated. This is NOT a single isolated reading.

Reflexes: Brisk bilaterally (+++). Two-beat ankle clonus present on the right — a sign of CNS irritability.
Face: Mild periorbital puffiness.
Legs: 2+ pitting oedema to mid-shin bilaterally.
Abdomen: Fundus =34cm, cephalic presentation, fetal heart 148 bpm by Doppler — reassuring.

History:
• No hypertension prior to pregnancy (BP 118/72 at booking at 10 weeks)
• At 28-week community review: BP 138/86 — documented, monitored, no further action taken
• Headache: 2 days, frontal, throbbing, unremitting, 6/10. Paracetamol ineffective.
• Visual symptoms: flashing lights and 'sparkles' in right visual field since this morning (photopsia)
• Mild nausea today. No vomiting.
• No right upper quadrant or epigastric pain.
• No vaginal bleeding. Fetal movements normal today.
• G1P0 — no prior pregnancies. No prior preeclampsia (family history: her mother had preeclampsia at term).
• No renal disease, no lupus, no antiphospholipid syndrome. No medications other than folic acid.

CLINICAL PICTURE: New hypertension after 20 weeks + headache + visual disturbance in a previously normotensive primigravida. Until proven otherwise, this is PREECLAMPSIA.

choices.text: Preeclampsia is my working diagnosis — order urgent investigations to confirm and quantify severity

effects.reason: Preeclampsia correctly identified as the working diagnosis based on clinical findings

choices.text: I recognise preeclampsia with severe features — start MgSO₄ and antihypertensives and call the obstetric registrar now

effects.reason: Preeclampsia correctly identified and management initiated without delay

Proceeding to treatment without baseline blood tests or urinalysis means no quantification of severity, no platelet count before MgSO₄, and no proteinuria documentation — these are needed for the clinical record and management decisions.

investigation-hub.text:
You have confirmed: BP 162/108 (×2), brisk reflexes, ankle clonus, headache, visual disturbances, 34+2 weeks gestation.

Working diagnosis: Preeclampsia — severity to be determined.

Severe features (ANY ONE is sufficient):
• BP ≥ 160/110 ✓
• Persistent headache ✓
• Visual disturbances ✓
• Thrombocytopenia (<100)
• Impaired renal or liver function
• Pulmonary oedema

What investigations do you want to order?

choices.text: Order urinalysis first — proteinuria is the key diagnostic test

effects.reason: Urinalysis ordered — correct initial investigation for suspected preeclampsia

choices.text: Order blood tests only (CBC, metabolic panel) — I'll check proteinuria later

effects.reason: Blood tests drawn
Proteinuria assessment is a mandatory component of preeclampsia diagnosis. Urinalysis should accompany any blood workup for suspected preeclampsia.

Blood tests drawn — essential for severity assessment, platelet count, and renal/liver function

choices.text: No tests needed — BP 162/108 with symptoms is sufficient for diagnosis. Assess severity now.

effects.reason: Skipping urinalysis and blood tests in suspected preeclampsia omits the proteinuria criterion, prevents platelet count assessment (clonus without thrombocytopenia changes MgSO₄ dosing), and misses HELLP syndrome. These tests take 15 minutes and must not be omitted.

urinalysis-result.text:
Urinalysis Result — RESULTED:

Appearance: Slightly cloudy, amber
Leukocyte esterase: Negative (no UTI)
Nitrites: Negative
Protein: +++ (3+) — SIGNIFICANT PROTEINURIA
Blood: Trace (non-specific)
Glucose: Negative

[!] Protein ≥ 2+ on dipstick is significant proteinuria in the context of hypertension.
[!] Protein 3+ represents ≥300mg/24h equivalent — meets diagnostic threshold for preeclampsia.

CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Hypertension (BP 162/108) + Significant Proteinuria (3+) + Symptoms (headache + visual disturbance) = PREECLAMPSIA CONFIRMED.

The urinalysis has confirmed the diagnosis. Now you must classify severity and initiate treatment.

effects.reason: Blood tests ordered to complete severity workup

choices.text: I have enough — BP 162/108 plus protein 3+ plus symptoms. Assess severity and initiate treatment.

bloods-result.text:
Blood Results — RESULTED:

CBC:
  WBC: 11.2 ×10⁹/L — mildly elevated (stress response)
  Haemoglobin: 11.4 g/dL — mildly low (dilutional in pregnancy)
  Platelets: 112 ×10⁹/L [↓] — borderline low (reference >150)
  • Platelets <100 would define severe features; 112 is borderline — watch closely

Metabolic Panel:
  Creatinine: 78 μmol/L — marginally elevated for pregnancy (normal in pregnancy <70)
  Urea: 4.8 mmol/L — mildly elevated
  Na: 136 mmol/L — normal
  K: 3.7 mmol/L — normal

Additional Labs (you have also requested):
  ALT: 62 U/L [↑] — elevated (reference <35 in pregnancy)
  AST: 48 U/L [↑] — elevated
  LDH: 420 U/L [↑] — elevated (reference <250)
  Uric acid: elevated
  CRP: 18 mg/L — mildly elevated
  Lactate: 1.4 mmol/L — normal (no tissue hypoperfusion yet)

SUMMARY: Borderline thrombocytopenia, mildly elevated LFTs, mild renal impairment. This laboratory picture is consistent with preeclampsia with features of developing HELLP syndrome (Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets). Platelet trend is critical — repeat in 4–6 hours.

choices.text: I now have the full picture — assess severity and classify this preeclampsia

severity-assessment.text:
SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION — PREECLAMPSIA:

You have the following findings:

• BP: 162/108 and 164/106 (×2 readings, 5 min apart)
• Proteinuria: 3+ on dipstick
• Headache: persistent, 2 days, unresponsive to paracetamol
• Visual disturbances: photopsia (flashing lights, right visual field)
• Reflexes: brisk +++, right ankle clonus 2 beats
• Platelets: 112 (borderline low)
• LFTs: mildly elevated
• Gestational age: 34+2 weeks

SEVERE FEATURES CRITERIA (ACOG/NICE):
✓ BP ≥ 160/110 (patient is 162/108 — YES)
✓ Persistent headache refractory to analgesia (YES)
✓ Visual disturbances — photopsia (YES)

She meets THREE independent severe feature criteria.

DIAGNOSTIC AMBIGUITY: 'The blood pressure is only 2mmHg above the threshold. She is awake, talking, and not in obvious distress. Perhaps this could be managed with oral antihypertensives and outpatient review?'

How do you classify this?

choices.text: SEVERE FEATURES CONFIRMED — triple criteria met (BP ≥160/110, persistent headache, visual disturbance). This requires immediate inpatient management with MgSO₄ prophylaxis and IV antihypertensives.

effects.reason: Severe features correctly identified — BP ≥160/110 is the threshold regardless of how close to 160 it is. Symptoms further solidify the classification.

choices.text: NOT severe features — BP is only just above 160, she is alert and comfortable. Admit for monitoring, oral antihypertensives, and outpatient repeat bloods in 24 hours.

effects.reason: This is a critical classification error. BP 162/108 IS ≥160/110 — the threshold is not approximate. Combined with persistent headache and visual disturbances, this patient has three independent severe feature criteria. Outpatient management of severe preeclampsia risks eclampsia, maternal stroke, and placental abruption.

observation-delay.text:
[DETERIORATION] Amara is admitted to the antenatal ward for 'monitoring.' An IV line is requested but not yet placed. No medications are started.

Thirty minutes pass.

The ward midwife calls you: 'Her BP is now 178/118. She's saying her head is going to explode. She's very agitated. I'm scared.'

You run to the ward.

As you push open the door, Amara suddenly goes silent. Then her eyes roll back. Her arms extend stiffly. Then — violent, rhythmic, tonic-clonic movements of her entire body.

She is seizing.

You have 90 seconds of convulsion in front of you.

choices.text: Call the emergency crash team and respond to the seizure

eclampsia-event.text:
[ECLAMPSIA — CODE OBSTETRIC] Amara Okonkwo is convulsing. Tonic-clonic seizure, generalised. She is not protecting her airway.

The room fills in seconds — the crash buzzer has been pressed. A crash trolley is at the door. The neonatal team has been called.

The fetal heart monitor is placed: fetal bradycardia — 92 bpm. The fetus is in distress.

You have a 78kg pregnant woman having an eclamptic seizure. You have IV access. The crash trolley is open in front of you.

BP: 178/118 | HR: 104 | SpO₂: 94% (seizing, semi-obstructed airway)

What is your immediate management?

choices.text: Left lateral position → oxygen via face mask → IV MgSO₄ 4g over 5 minutes to terminate seizure → IV labetalol 20mg for BP control → call OB/anaesthetics immediately

effects.reason: MgSO₄ given — first-line treatment for eclampsia AND seizure termination. Both therapeutic and prophylactic.
IV labetalol given for acute severe hypertension during eclampsia
OB and anaesthetics called for eclampsia — appropriate emergency escalation

choices.text: Left lateral position → IV diazepam 10mg to stop the seizure → call for help

effects.reason: Diazepam is not first-line for eclampsia. MgSO₄ is the drug of choice for both treating eclampsia AND preventing recurrence. Diazepam has no role in further seizure prophylaxis. MgSO₄ must still be given.
OB team called for eclampsia

choices.text: Step back — most eclamptic seizures self-terminate within 90 seconds. Wait for it to stop before intervening.

effects.reason: An eclamptic seizure is a medical emergency. Waiting without airway protection or MgSO₄ risks maternal hypoxia, aspiration, placental abruption, and fetal hypoxic injury. Immediate intervention is mandatory.

management-hub.text:
SEVERE PREECLAMPSIA — IMMEDIATE TREATMENT REQUIRED.

Current status:
• BP: 162/108 (×2)
• Proteinuria: 3+
• Symptoms: Persistent headache + visual disturbance
• Reflexes: Brisk +++, ankle clonus
• Fetal heart: 148 bpm (reassuring at this point)
• Gestational age: 34+2 weeks

ACOG / NICE guidance:
→ MgSO₄: Give a loading dose for eclampsia prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia
→ Antihypertensives: BP ≥160/110 requires acute treatment within 30–60 minutes to reduce maternal stroke risk. Target 140–150/90–100.
→ Senior obstetric review: Delivery is the only definitive treatment. Timing must be decided by the specialist team.

What is your immediate management plan?

choices.text: MgSO₄ 4g IV loading dose over 15 minutes + IV labetalol 20mg for BP ≥160/110 + urgent OB registrar/consultant + continuous CTG for fetal monitoring

optimal-management.text:
The on-call obstetric registrar, Dr. Yemi Adeyemi, arrives within eight minutes and reviews Amara.

'Good call. This is severe preeclampsia. She meets severe feature criteria on three counts.'

Current status after initial treatment:
BP: 144/92 (down from 162/108 — within target)
HR: 82 | SpO₂: 99%
MgSO₄: Loading dose complete, maintenance infusion 1g/hour commenced
CTG: Reactive at 148 bpm — reassuring fetal pattern

Dr. Adeyemi explains the plan to Amara:

'Your blood pressure has been dangerously high and it has been affecting your body. We need to deliver your baby. At 34 weeks, he is very likely to do well — the neonatal team is already aware. We're going to talk about how we do that.

You could try induction of labour, or we could plan a caesarean section. I'll explain both options. But we need to be in theatre within the next few hours.'

Amara nods, her headache already slightly better. 'Whatever is safest for the baby.'

Your role is to confirm the handover and document the clinical management appropriately.

effects.reason: Delivery planning initiated with specialist obstetric team — appropriate definitive management of severe preeclampsia at 34+ weeks

choices.text: Confirm the handover, document fully, and ensure postnatal monitoring is arranged

outcome-excellent.text:
Amara Okonkwo undergoes induction of labour at 34+2 weeks. After 9 hours of augmented labour, she delivers a live male infant weighing 2.12kg. Apgar scores: 8 at 1 minute, 9 at 5 minutes.

The baby is taken to the neonatal unit for monitoring — likely 2–3 weeks. He is breathing independently.

MgSO₄ is continued for 24 hours postpartum.

Amara's blood pressure normalises progressively over the next 48 hours. She is transferred to the postnatal ward on day 2. Antihypertensives are weaned over 6 weeks of community follow-up.

--- Final Results ---
BP at discharge (Day 4): 132/84 — improving trend
Platelet nadir: 108 — did not drop below 100
LFTs: normalising at Day 3 review
Baby: Discharged to mother at Day 19 — feeding well

Amara visits the postnatal clinic at 6 weeks. 'He's beautiful,' she says, showing you the photo. 'And I feel completely normal again.'

[!] Teaching Points:
• BP ≥160/110 in pregnancy = acute severe hypertension = treat within 30–60 minutes — no debate
• MgSO₄ reduces the risk of eclampsia by ~50% in severe preeclampsia and is FIRST-LINE for eclampsia treatment
• Persistent headache + visual disturbances = severe features — even if the patient looks 'well'
• Delivery is the only cure for preeclampsia. At ≥34 weeks with severe features, delivery is indicated.
• Midwives often recognise preeclampsia early — listen to experienced clinical colleagues

outcome-eclampsia-survived.text:
The eclamptic seizure terminates after 2 minutes following MgSO₄ administration.

Amara is left post-ictal — drowsy, confused, and exhausted. The fetal bradycardia resolves as her oxygenation improves.

Emergency caesarean section is performed under general anaesthesia. A live male infant is delivered, 2.08kg. He requires CPAP initially but is breathing independently by 2 hours of life.

Amara recovers in HDU for 48 hours. She develops a brief period of pulmonary oedema on night 1, managed with furosemide. Her renal function deteriorates mildly before recovering by Day 5.

--- Results ---
Maternal: Full recovery, discharged Day 7
Neonatal: NICU 22 days, discharged to mother in good condition
Platelet nadir: 91 (×10⁹/L) — confirmed HELLP syndrome

Eclampsia is a life-threatening emergency that was precipitated by delayed recognition of severe features. The seizure itself caused fetal distress, altered the delivery plan, and required HDU care.

[!] Teaching Points:
• The window between 'stable severe preeclampsia' and 'eclampsia' is narrow and unpredictable
• MgSO₄ in severe preeclampsia would have prevented this seizure in approximately 50% of cases
• HELLP syndrome can develop rapidly once liver enzymes and platelets are trending abnormally
• Every hour's delay in treating severe features increases maternal and fetal risk

outcome-fatal.text:
The seizure lasts 4 minutes without intervention. By the time the team assembles, Amara has aspirated and her oxygen saturation is 74%.

The fetal heart has been in sustained bradycardia at 68 bpm for 6 minutes.

Despite emergency intubation, crash caesarean, and resuscitation:
• The baby is delivered with Apgar 1 and 1 — severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
• Amara suffers a right MCA haemorrhagic stroke during the resuscitation, secondary to her uncontrolled blood pressure

She survives with severe right-sided weakness and aphasia. Her son survives with profound neurodisability.

The coroner's investigation identifies unrecognised and untreated preeclampsia with severe features as the avoidable precipitating cause.

[!] Teaching Points:
• Eclampsia is PREVENTABLE in most cases with timely MgSO₄
• An eclamptic seizure without immediate intervention causes maternal hypoxia, fetal distress, and risks maternal stroke from surging blood pressure
• 'Waiting for the seizure to stop' is not a management plan — it is an abandonment of management
• Preeclampsia kills. The tools to prevent it are simple, cheap, and available. The barrier is recognition and timely action.
